elements.quote: We performed a systematic search of MEDLINE, OVID Epub and EMBASE databases for English language literature from 2019 to April 16, 2020.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states that a systematic search was performed, identifying the work as a systematic review-type effort.

elements.quote: Aims: To determine the prevalence of bacterial co-infection (at presentation) and secondary infection (after presentation) in patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract gives a clear, explicit statement of the main objective/review question.

elements.quote: Studies were included if they (a) evaluated patients with confirmed COVID-19 and (b) reported the prevalence of acute bacterial infection. Any bacteria detected from non-respiratory-tract or non-bloodstream sources were excluded.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies main inclusion criteria and an exclusion criterion regarding non-respiratory/non-bloodstream bacterial detections.

elements.quote: We performed a systematic search of MEDLINE, OVID Epub and EMBASE databases for English language literature from 2019 to April 16, 2020.
elements.reason: The abstract names the information sources searched and gives the last search date (April 16, 2020).
The abstract does not describe any methods used to assess risk of bias in included studies.

elements.quote: In the meta-analysis, bacterial co-infection (estimated on presentation) was identified in 3.5% of patients (95%CI 0.4 e 6.7%) and secondary bacterial infection in 14.3% of patients (95%CI 9.6 e 18.9%).
elements.reason: The abstract indicates that a meta-analysis was conducted and presents synthesized results, but does not specify the synthesis methods (e.g. random-effects model) or how results were presented beyond reporting proportions and CIs.

elements.quote: Of 1308 studies screened, 24 were eligible and included in the rapid review representing 3338 patients with COVID-19 evaluated for acute bacterial infection.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and participants and gives summary study counts/characteristics.

elements.quote: In the meta-analysis, bacterial co-infection (estimated on presentation) was identified in 3.5% of patients (95%CI 0.4 e 6.7%) and secondary bacterial infection in 14.3% of patients (95%CI 9.6 e 18.9%). The overall proportion of COVID-19 patients with bacterial infection was 6.9% (95%CI 4.3 e 9.5%).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes with estimates and confidence intervals, and the overall participant/sample numbers are reported elsewhere in the abstract.

elements.quote: In the meta-analysis, bacterial co-infection (estimated on presentation) was identified in 3.5% of patients (95%CI 0.4 e 6.7%) and secondary bacterial infection in 14.3% of patients (95%CI 9.6 e 18.9%).
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports summary estimates with confidence intervals.

elements.quote: Bacterial infection was more common in critically ill patients (8.1%, 95%CI 2.3 e 13.8%).
elements.reason: When comparing groups (critically ill vs others), the abstract indicates the direction of effect (more common in critically ill patients).
The abstract does not briefly summarize limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision).

elements.quote: Implications: Bacterial co-infection is relatively infrequent in hospitalized patients with COVID-19. The majority of these patients may not require empirical antibacterial treatment.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and their implications for practice.
The abstract does not report the primary source of funding for the review.
Although the protocol registration (PROSPERO ID CRD42020180229) appears in the Methods section (text_5), the abstract itself does not provide the register name or registration number.

elements.quote: The prevalence, incidence and characteristics of bacterial infection in patients infected with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is not well understood and has been raised as an important knowledge gap [6,7].
elements.reason: The introduction explicitly states the current state of knowledge is limited and identifies an important knowledge gap regarding prevalence, incidence and characteristics of bacterial infection in SARS-CoV-2.

elements.quote: Understanding the proportion of COVID-19 patients with acute respiratory bacterial co-infection, and the culprit pathogens, is crucial for treating patients with COVID-19 and to help ensure responsible use of antibiotics and to minimize negative consequences of overuse [6]. In addition, this knowledge could have a significant impact in refining empirical antibiotic management guidelines for patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The introduction explains why the review is needed: to inform patient treatment, promote responsible antibiotic use, and refine empirical antibiotic guidelines.

elements.quote: Our findings are consistent with those of a recent systematic review and meta-analysis that included 30 studies evaluating coinfections among patients infected with COVID-19. Similarly, the authors reported that 7% of patients had a bacterial co-infection ... Our study adds to this literature by estimating co-infection versus secondary infection prevalence and by updating the evaluation throughout the pandemic.
elements.reason: The discussion acknowledges existing systematic reviews, cites them, and explains how the current review adds new value (separating co-infection vs secondary infection and providing an ongoing/updating assessment).
The review assesses prevalence of bacterial co-infection in COVID-19 and is not a review of intervention effects; no intervention mechanism is proposed in the manuscript.
The review does not evaluate complex interventions or delivery contexts and does not present or discuss a logic model; requirement not applicable to this prevalence-focused review.

elements.quote: Aims: To determine the prevalence of bacterial co-infection (at presentation) and secondary infection (after presentation) in patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract contains an explicit statement of the review objective specifying the population (patients with COVID-19) and the outcomes of interest (prevalence of bacterial co-infection and secondary infection).

elements.quote: We conducted a rapid systematic review guided by recommendations from the Cochrane Rapid Reviews Methods Group [10] to determine the prevalence of respiratory bacterial infections among individuals with con fi rmed active COVID-19 infection.
elements.reason: The review addresses prevalence of bacterial infection rather than effects of interventions, so planned comparisons using PICO for intervention effects do not apply.

elements.quote: We included studies of humans with laboratory-con fi rmed SARS-CoV-2 infection across all healthcare settings (i.e. hospital, community, long-term care) and age groups (paediatric and adult patients). Bacterial infection was de fi ned as an acute infection including either (a) co-infection on presentation, or (b) secondary infection emerging during the course of illness or hospital stay. Cases where bacteria were detected in an isolate not from a respiratory tract or blood culture sample were excluded. We included randomized controlled trials, cohort studies and case series with more than 10 patients, but excluded reviews, editorials, letters and case studies. We considered studies to be eligible regardless of experimental or observational design, and irrespective of their primary objective. However, we excluded studies that did not report data on bacterial infection or exclusively reported data on chronic co-infection or non-bacterial pathogens.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly list the population (humans with lab-confirmed SARS-CoV-2), settings, age groups, definition of bacterial infection (co-infection vs secondary), specimen restrictions, eligible study designs and explicit exclusions and reporting requirements.

elements.quote: We performed a systematic search of MEDLINE, OVID Epub and EMBASE databases for published literature in the English language from January 1, 2019 to April 16, 2020 with assistance from a medical library information specialist.
elements.reason: The report specifies language (English) and a date range for included reports, and refers to searching published literature (publication status).

Evidence notes that studies were excluded for lack of reporting of bacterial infection data, but does not distinguish exclusions because outcomes were not measured versus outcomes measured but not reported; no explicit statement separating these two reasons is provided.

elements.quote: Seven studies exclusively reported secondary bacterial infections, the remaining 17 studies were categorized as reporting bacterial co-infection. ... When strati fi ed by patient population (an estimate of COVID-19 illness severity), bacterial infection ranged from 5.9% (95%CI 3.8 e 8.0%) in all hospitalized patients to 8.1% in critically ill patients (95%CI 2.3 e 13.8) (Fig. 3).
elements.reason: The review specifies groupings used in syntheses (studies categorized as co-infection vs secondary infection and stratification by patient population/illness severity) and links these to the comparisons/estimates presented.

elements.quote: A rapid review was selected as the ideal methodology to synthesize knowledge in a timely fashion for this emergent issue, so that learnings could impact clinical care during the ongoing pandemic.
elements.reason: The authors provide a rationale for using a rapid review approach (a notable methodological restriction). However, while many specific eligibility restrictions are listed (e.g. specimen types excluded, minimum case series size, exclusion of reviews/letters), explicit rationales for those specific restrictions are not provided in the evidence.

elements.quote: We performed a systematic search of MEDLINE, OVID Epub and EMBASE databases for published literature in the English language from January 1, 2019 to April 16, 2020 with assistance from a medical library information specialist.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the date range and the end date of the search (April 16, 2020), fulfilling the requirement to report when the information sources were last searched/consulted.

elements.quote: We performed a systematic search of MEDLINE, OVID Epub and EMBASE databases for published literature in the English language from January 1, 2019 to April 16, 2020 with assistance from a medical library information specialist.
elements.reason: The names of bibliographic databases (MEDLINE, OVID Epub, EMBASE) and a platform/interface reference (OVID Epub) are provided, and the search date range is given; however, the available coverage dates for each database (their indexing coverage periods) are not reported.
No study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories searched are named in the provided evidence; no names or date restrictions are reported.

elements.quote: The results of the search were imported into Covidence (Covidence, Melbourne, Australia), an online software tool for systematic reviews.
elements.reason: Although Covidence (an online tool) is mentioned for managing results, the evidence does not report any websites, search engines, or online sources that were searched as information sources with their names and URLs; thus the requirement to report websites/URLs searched is not met.
There is no evidence that organisations or manufacturers were contacted to identify studies; no organisations are named as being contacted.
No types of individuals contacted to identify studies are described in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The reference section of articles selected for inclusion were handsearched by an author (BL) to identify any additional studies for potential inclusion.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies that the reference sections of included articles were handsearched, which describes the type of reference lists examined.

elements.quote: The reference section of articles selected for inclusion were handsearched by an author (BL) to identify any additional studies for potential inclusion.
elements.reason: Backward citation searching (handsearching reference sections) is reported, but the manuscript does not report the seed reports, citation index/platform used, or the date when this citation searching was performed.
No journals or conference proceedings consulted are named, and no dates covered or search methods for such sources are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: All titles and abstracts were independently screened by two authors (BL, VL) to determine whether studies met the inclusion criteria; all full-text studies meeting these criteria were then reviewed by two authors (BL and MS or SR) for final inclusion in the rapid review.
elements.reason: Explicitly reports the number of reviewers for title/abstract screening (two) and for full-text review (two).

elements.quote: All titles and abstracts were independently screened by two authors (BL, VL) to determine whether studies met the inclusion criteria; all full-text studies meeting these criteria were then reviewed by two authors (BL and MS or SR) for final inclusion in the rapid review.
elements.reason: Independence is explicitly stated for title/abstract screening but the full-text review is described as "reviewed by two authors" without explicitly stating they worked independently.

elements.quote: Disagreements that could not be resolved via consensus were reviewed independently by an additional author.
elements.reason: Describes the process for resolving screening disagreements (consensus, and unresolved disagreements adjudicated by an additional independent author).
No description found of processes used to obtain or confirm eligibility information from study investigators.
No methods reported for translating abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment.

elements.quote: The results of the search were imported into Covidence (Covidence, Melbourne, Australia), an online software tool for systematic reviews. Duplicate records were removed using Covidence.
elements.reason: Names an automation tool (Covidence) and explicitly states its role in importing search results and removing duplicate records in the selection process.
No information on externally derived classifiers (versions/references, roles) or records removed before screening.
No information on internally derived classifiers, their training, validation, or use.
No description of machine-learning prioritisation tools or stopping/prioritisation rules.
No reporting of crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection.
No description of previously screened datasets used to eliminate records.

elements.quote: Two authors performed data extraction from included studies using a spreadsheet, and cross-checked for accuracy and completeness (DW, BL).
elements.reason: Explicitly reports the number of reviewers who collected data (two) and names initials of those reviewers.

elements.quote: Two authors performed data extraction from included studies using a spreadsheet, and cross-checked for accuracy and completeness (DW, BL).
elements.reason: Although multiple data collectors are named, the text does not state whether they worked independently during data extraction.

elements.quote: Two authors performed data extraction from included studies using a spreadsheet, and cross-checked for accuracy and completeness (DW, BL).
elements.reason: No description is provided of processes used to resolve disagreements between data collectors for data extraction.
No information is provided about processes used to obtain or confirm data from study investigators.

elements.quote: The results of the search were imported into Covidence (Covidence, Melbourne, Australia), an online software tool for systematic reviews. Duplicate records were removed using Covidence.
elements.reason: While Covidence is mentioned for importing search results and deduplication, there is no description of automation tools specifically used for data collection, nor details of their use, training, or validation.
No methods for translating articles for data collection are reported in the provided evidence.
No software or methods for extracting data from figures are specified in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: To avoid duplication of patient data, each study was captured only once, reporting either co-infection or secondary infection data, whichever component was larger.
elements.reason: Provides a decision rule for selecting data from multiple reports and resolving potential duplicate data.

elements.quote: The main outcome of interest was the overall proportion of confirmed acute bacterial infections in patients with COVID-19 stratified by co-infection on initial presentation and secondary infection during the course of the illness. We also stratified bacterial infection rates by patient population as an estimate of the severity of COVID-19 illness, as: (a) all hospitalized patients or (b) critically ill patients (admitted to intensive care unit). Studies were categorized as reporting co-infection (bacterial infection on presentation) unless they explicitly stated that they were capturing secondary infection data by using the term 'secondary infection' or indicating that infection data were captured after admission. To avoid duplication of patient data, each study was captured only once, reporting either co-infection or secondary infection data, whichever component was larger.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists and defines the primary outcomes (overall proportion of confirmed acute bacterial infections, stratified by co-infection on presentation vs secondary infection during illness) and specifies the time context (on presentation vs during course). It also states whether all compatible results were sought and describes the selection rule used when studies reported both (capturing each study only once and choosing the larger component), fulfilling the requirement to specify methods for selecting results.

elements.quote: The following variables were extracted: country of study, start and end date of study, healthcare site name(s), study design (retrospective versus prospective), healthcare setting, sample size, age group, patient population, mean or median age, proportion of female patients, disease severity, proportion of patients requiring mechanical ventilation, proportion of patients that were smokers, reported comorbidities (i.e., chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cardiovascular disease, hypertension), bacteriological testing methods, patients with acute respiratory co-infection, proportion of patients with secondary bacterial infection, respiratory organisms identi fi ed and their proportions, bacterial susceptibility, viral testing methods, proportion of patients receiving antibiotics and class of antibiotic.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists and defines a comprehensive set of additional variables extracted from included studies.

elements.quote: Studies reporting concomitant bacterial pathogens in COVID-19 were assumed to represent co-infection rather than secondary infection.
elements.reason: The authors state an explicit assumption about how to classify studies that reported concomitant bacterial pathogens (treating them as co-infection), addressing assumptions for unclear information.

No citation or description is provided of a specific tool used to determine which data items to collect (the authors report using a spreadsheet for extraction and cite review guidance and screening software elsewhere, but do not cite a tool that determined the data-item list).

elements.quote: Assessment of bias A formal assessment for risk of bias was deemed to have limited utility given the lack of an appropriate assessment tool. Although a risk-of-bias tool has been developed for meta-analyses of disease prevalence [14], many aspects of the tool are not directly relevant to our research question.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states a formal risk-of-bias assessment was not performed and does not specify any risk-of-bias tool or version.

elements.quote: Therefore, we incorporated study quality into our sensitivity analysis based on three key factors: whether bacterial diagnostic method was reported, whether co-infection was explicitly subcategorized (i.e. co-infection versus secondary infection), and with removal of studies with potentially overlapping patient cohorts.
elements.reason: While no formal risk-of-bias tool was used, the authors specify three study-quality factors that they used in sensitivity analyses; however these are not presented as domains/components of a standard risk-of-bias tool.

elements.quote: Assessment of bias A formal assessment for risk of bias was deemed to have limited utility given the lack of an appropriate assessment tool.
elements.reason: The authors state they did not perform a formal risk-of-bias assessment and do not report any overall risk-of-bias judgments or rules for deriving such judgments.

elements.quote: A formal assessment for risk of bias was deemed to have limited utility given the lack of an appropriate assessment tool.
elements.reason: No existing risk-of-bias tool was applied, so there are no reported adaptations to an existing tool.

elements.quote: A formal assessment for risk of bias was deemed to have limited utility given the lack of an appropriate assessment tool.
elements.reason: The manuscript does not describe development or use of any newly developed risk-of-bias tool.

elements.reason: The item requests number of reviewers, independence, and disagreement-resolution procedures for risk-of-bias assessment; because no formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed, these required details are not reported.

elements.quote: A formal assessment for risk of bias was deemed to have limited utility given the lack of an appropriate assessment tool.
elements.reason: The manuscript does not describe any processes to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators.

elements.quote: A formal assessment for risk of bias was deemed to have limited utility given the lack of an appropriate assessment tool.
elements.reason: No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment are described; the authors indicate no formal risk-of-bias assessment was conducted.

elements.quote: We pooled proportion data across studies using a random effects meta-analysis with the DerSimonian e Laird method [12].
elements.reason: The methods explicitly state that pooled proportion data were used and synthesized via random-effects meta-analysis; results report proportions with 95% CIs (e.g. 'In the random effects meta-analysis bacterial co-infection was identified in 3.5% of patients (95%CI 0.4 e 6.7%)') indicating the effect measure is the proportion (with CIs).

No thresholds or ranges are reported for interpreting effect size (magnitude of proportions) or their rationale. The manuscript reports heterogeneity I2 thresholds, but does not provide thresholds/ranges for interpreting the effect sizes themselves.
The manuscript does not describe any methods to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure.
No justification for the choice of effect measure (why proportions were chosen) is provided in the available evidence.

elements.quote: Studies were categorized as reporting co-infection (bacterial infection on presentation) unless they explicitly stated that they were capturing secondary infection data by using the term ' secondary infection ' or indicating that infection data were captured after admission. To avoid duplication of patient data, each study was captured only once, reporting either co-infection or secondary infection data, whichever component was larger.
elements.reason: The Data Synthesis section describes the rules used to decide which studies contributed to each synthesis (how studies were categorized as co-infection vs secondary infection and how duplicate data were handled), which directly explains processes for eligibility for each synthesis.

elements.quote: We pooled proportion data across studies using a random effects meta-analysis with the DerSimonian e Laird method [12]. Results were illustrated using forest plots. Heterogeneity was assessed by I 2 statistic, with < 40% considered low heterogeneity, 30 e 60% considered moderate heterogeneity, 50 e 90% considered substantial heterogeneity, and 75 e 100% considered considerable heterogeneity [13]. All analyses were carried out using R version 3.6.0 with the packages metafor and meta .
elements.reason: The manuscript describes some data-preparation and synthesis methods (pooling proportions using a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects meta-analysis, heterogeneity assessment, software/packages). However, it does not describe handling of missing summary statistics or any data conversions, so the reporting is incomplete for this item.

elements.quote: All analyses were carried out using R version 3.6.0 with the packages metafor and meta .
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the software (R 3.6.0) and packages (metafor, meta) used for statistical synthesis.
No description or justification of alternative synthesis/summarization methods when meta-analysis was not possible is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We pooled proportion data across studies using a random effects meta-analysis with the DerSimonian e Laird method [12].
elements.reason: The meta-analysis model (random-effects using DerSimonian–Laird) is reported, but no explicit rationale for choosing this model is provided in the available text.

elements.quote: We pooled proportion data across studies using a random effects meta-analysis with the DerSimonian e Laird method [12]. Results were illustrated using forest plots.
elements.reason: The statistical method used for the meta-analysis (random-effects meta-analysis with DerSimonian–Laird) and presentation (forest plots) are explicitly described.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity was assessed by I 2 statistic, with < 40% considered low heterogeneity, 30 e 60% considered moderate heterogeneity, 50 e 90% considered substantial heterogeneity, and 75 e 100% considered considerable heterogeneity [13].
elements.reason: The manuscript states the heterogeneity metric used (I-squared) and the thresholds applied to interpret heterogeneity.

elements.quote: We pooled proportion data across studies using a random effects meta-analysis with the DerSimonian e Laird method [12].
elements.reason: The between-study variance estimator for the random-effects meta-analysis is specified (DerSimonian–Laird).

No method for calculating confidence intervals for the summary effect (e.g., Hartung-Knapp, normal approximation) is specified in the provided text; CIs are reported but the CI calculation method is not described.

Some additional random-effects details (reported τ² and heterogeneity test statistics) are shown in the forest-plot figure, but the methods section does not comprehensively describe other implementation details (e.g., weighting scheme, continuity corrections), so reporting of such implementation details is partial.

elements.quote: We pooled proportion data across studies using a random effects meta-analysis with the DerSimonian e Laird method [12].
elements.reason: The analysis is frequentist (DerSimonian–Laird random-effects); no Bayesian meta-analysis was performed, so reporting of Bayesian priors is not applicable.

elements.quote: To avoid duplication of patient data, each study was captured only once, reporting either co-infection or secondary infection data, whichever component was larger.
elements.reason: The authors describe a method to avoid dependency from duplicated patient data by capturing each study only once and choosing the larger component, addressing statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study.
No explicit identification in the retrieved evidence of planned syntheses that were judged impossible or inappropriate, nor reasons for such decisions.

elements.quote: We pooled proportion data across studies using a random effects meta-analysis with the DerSimonian e Laird method [12]. Results were illustrated using forest plots. Heterogeneity was assessed by I 2 statistic, with < 40% considered low heterogeneity, 30 e 60% considered moderate heterogeneity, 50 e 90% considered substantial heterogeneity, and 75 e 100% considered considerable heterogeneity [13]. All analyses were carried out using R version 3.6.0 with the packages metafor and meta . ... Therefore, we incorporated study quality into our sensitivity analysis based on three key factors: whether bacterial diagnostic method was reported, whether co-infection was explicitly subcategorized (i.e. co-infection versus secondary infection), and with removal of studies with potentially overlapping patient cohorts.
elements.reason: The methods section specifies that heterogeneity was assessed (I2) and describes planned sensitivity analyses/approaches to explore heterogeneity (stratifying by diagnostic method, co-infection vs secondary, and removing overlapping cohorts).

elements.quote: When strati fi ed by patient population (an estimate of COVID-19 illness severity), bacterial infection ranged from 5.9% (95%CI 3.8 e 8.0%) in all hospitalized patients to 8.1% in critically ill patients (95%CI 2.3 e 13.8) ... The proportion of COVID-19 patients with bacterial infection differed based on the reported method of testing: 4.6% (95%CI 0.9 e 8.2) for culture, 4.4% (95%CI 0.0 e 14.0) for nucleic acid amplifi cation and 9.6% (95%CI 5.9 e 13.3) when the method was not speci fi ed (Appendix Fig. A). In a sensitivity analysis where studies were strati fi ed by those explicitly and those not explicitly distinguishing co-infection from secondary infection, there was negligible difference in the reported prevalence of bacterial infection: 4.6% (95%CI 0.2 e 9.0%) and 2.5% (95%CI 0.0 e 7.9%), respectively (Appendix Fig. B).

elements.quote:
Sensitivity analyses
The proportion of COVID-19 patients with bacterial infection differed based on the reported method of testing: 4.6% (95%CI 0.9 e 8.2) for culture, 4.4% (95%CI 0.0 e 14.0) for nucleic acid amplifi cation and 9.6% (95%CI 5.9 e 13.3) when the method was not speci fi ed (Appendix Fig. A). Studies reporting concomitant bacterial pathogens in COVID-19 were assumed to represent co-infection rather than secondary infection. In a sensitivity analysis where studies were strati fi ed by those explicitly and those not explicitly distinguishing co-infection from secondary infection, there was negligible difference in the reported prevalence of bacterial infection: 4.6% (95%CI 0.2 e 9.0%) and 2.5% (95%CI 0.0 e 7.9%), respectively (Appendix Fig. B). Of 24 studies included, nine contained potential duplicate data due to overlapping hospital site, patient age group and study time period. Removing any potential duplicate study cohorts did not signi fi cantly change the estimate of bacterial co-infection (3.8%, 95%CI 0.0 e 8.0%), secondary infection (14.3%, 95%CI 8.9 e 19.7%), or the overall proportion with bacterial infection (7.7%, 95%CI 4.4 e 11.1%) compared to original estimates (Appendix Fig. C).

elements.quote: However, this review and meta-analysis also has important limitations. While we identified 24 studies representing over 3000 patients, bacterial infections in patients with COVID-19 disease may be under- or over-represented, as there was a lack of consistent bacteriological diagnostic method and a specific testing method was not reported in half of all the studies. Further, distinguishing bacterial colonization from infection presents a challenge, particularly in the context of COVID-19 infection. We only examined the subset of COVID-19 studies that reported the presence or absence of bacterial infections, and the temporal relationship between bacterial and viral infection was not explicit; hence differentiating co-infection from secondary infection was challenging. In addition, we did not perform a formal assessment for risk of bias. However, we attempted to address these limitations through our three sensitivity analyses, which remained robust to our initial estimates. The generalizability of our estimates may be limited as the majority of studies were from Asia during the start of the pandemic. Regional variations in patient population, access to care, and infection prevention and control are all potential variables that could impact the likelihood of bacterial co-infection and secondary infection. To overcome this limitation, we are planning a living meta-analysis with regular systematic searches to better inform our co-infection and secondary infection estimates, which will be hosted on the Toronto Antimicrobial Resistance Research Network (TARRN) website (https://www.tarrn.org/covid). Lastly, the estimates in our metaanalysis were primarily based on hospitalized adult patients, and may not reflect the overall bacterial infection rates as the vast majority of COVID-19 patients experience mild disease and do not require hospitalization [52].
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly lists multiple limitations of the included evidence (inconsistent diagnostic methods, inability to distinguish colonization vs infection, unclear temporal relationship, no formal risk-of-bias assessment, limited geographic/generalizability, and focus on hospitalized adults).
